marks: Makkhali Gosala, born nearby, is generally considered the founder; the city was the hub of the Ājīvikas.
Ashoka's dedications of cave halls to the Ājīvikas date from the 12th and 19th years of his reign.
Inscriptions record a tax on the Ājīvikas, the last dated 1346 CE.
The last dated inscription that records a tax on Ājīvikas or Acuvas.
notes: Makkhali Gosala, a contemporary of the Buddha and Mahavira, is generally considered the founder of the Ājīvikas, who are known from Buddhist and Jain texts to have centred on Savatthi.
The Ājīvikas spread to Gujarat and to Sri Lanka, where they have a community centre, by the 4th century BCE.
Ashoka dedicates the Barabar Caves in Bihar to the Ājīvikas, whose school is said to have been favoured by his father Bindusara.
After the decline of the Maurya Empire the Ājīvikas find only occasional mention in Sanskrit literature.
In northern India the Ājīvikas may have become insignificant, and references in the Vayu Purana suggest a rapid decline under the Guptas.
Inscriptions in southern India, from the time of the Pallava king Simhavarman II, record a tax on Ājīvikas or Acuvas.
The Jain commentator Mallisena suggests that the Ājīvikas still exist, perhaps knowing those of southern India.
The last dated tax inscription, around Kolar, is set up; later references suggest survival to the 15th century at most.
src: A. L. Basham, History and Doctrines of the Ājīvikas (Luzac, 1951)
Piotr Balcerowicz, Early Asceticism in India: Ājīvikism and Jainism (Routledge, 2015)
